query: Earlier refractory high-entropy alloys illustrate persistent trade-offs: MoNbTaW and MoNbTaVW retained good yield strength from 600 to 1600 °C, with MoNbTaVW reaching 842 MPa at 1000 °C, but both had poor room-temperature fracture toughness and high density; HfNbTaTiZr showed room-temperature ductility above 50% and a yield strength of 929 MPa but only 295 MPa at 1000 °C; and as-cast HfMoTaTiZr achieved about 1600 MPa at room temperature and 855 MPa at elevated temperature but retained a density of 10.21 g cm−3. Given the constraint that density must be reduced without sacrificing the strong room- and high-temperature mechanical performance of as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, what single intervention should be tested? Provide a mechanistic hypothesis, predicted outcomes relative to the as-cast baseline, explicit temperature and loading boundary conditions, supporting evidence from the preceding RHEA results, and a controlled experiment with quantitative rejection criteria that could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Substitution of heavier elements with lighter ones, such as replacing Mo with V, in the as-cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy will reduce its density without sacrificing its strong room- and high-temperature mechanical performance.
generation.conditions: room temperature to 1600 °C, yield strength and fracture toughness
generation.predicted_outcome: reduced density by 5-10% while maintaining yield strength above 1500 MPa at room temperature and 800 MPa at 1000 °C
generation.baseline: as-cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy with a density of 10.21 g cm−3
generation.boundary: temperature range from room temperature to 1600 °C, loading conditions of yield strength and fracture toughness
generation.uncertainty: the exact amount of density reduction and the resulting mechanical properties may vary depending on the specific substitution ratio and processing conditions

falsification_experiment.design: prepare alloy samples with varying substitution ratios of Mo with V, measure their density and mechanical properties at room and elevated temperatures
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: if the density reduction is less than 3% or the yield strength at room temperature is less than 1400 MPa, the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are a relatively new class of multicomponent materials that are based on several refractory metals, but may also contain other, generally low density, elements and typically have a body centered cubic (BCC) crystal structure [1] – [3] . These alloys have recently received much attention because of their attractive combination of properties not achievable by other classes of metallic alloys. For example, the first two RHEAs, NbMoTaW and NbMoTaVW, showed weak temperature dependence of yield strength in the temperature range from 600 °C to 1600 °C, with yield strength above 400 MPa at 1600 °C [4] , [5] . Unfortunately, these two alloys had high density (>12 g/cm 3 ) and further developments aimed at reducing the alloy density while keeping superior high-temperature properties. In the second generation RHEAs, high-density Ta and W were replaced with lower density refractory elements, such as Cr, Mo, Nb, V and Zr, and low density Al and Ti were added [6] – [13] . Recently the concept of high-entropy alloys (HEAs), consisting of four or more principle metallic elements in equiatomic or near-equiatomic ratios, has attracted considerable interest owing to its tendency to form solid solution with outstanding mechanical and functional properties [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. By introducing refractory elements including group IV (Ti, Zr, and Hf), V (V, Nb, and Ta), and VI (Cr, Mo, and W) in HEAs, the developed refractory HEAs (RHEAs) possess high melting temperature, outstanding strength and hardness, high thermal stability, and softening resistance at elevated temperatures, which opens up the possibilities of the alloy developments satisfying structural demands at high temperature.

Since the first WMoTaNb RHEA was reported in 2010, many literatures have been focused on the preparation methods and mechanical properties of RHEAs [ [7] , [8] ]. For example, the BCC WMoTaNb and WMoTaNbV HEAs maintained yield strength of 405 and 477 MPa at 1600 °C respectively, which were much higher than that of Inconel 718 and Haynes 230 [ [9] ].
